article.overview: An elemental composition analyser is an instrument that identifies which chemical elements are present in lunar material and, in many designs, estimates how much of each element is present. The Moon has been investigated with this class of instrument from lunar orbit and from landers and rovers on the surface. The catalogue entry describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The main measurement principles used in lunar and planetary work are alpha-particle backscattering, alpha-induced X-ray emission, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence and gamma-ray spectroscopy [1][2][7].
article.description: An elemental composition analyser examines a small area of lunar material, usually the regolith (the loose surface layer) or exposed rock, and converts the response of that material into a spectrum. Each chemical element produces a characteristic signal, such as an X-ray of a particular energy, a light emission at particular wavelengths, or scattered particles that lose a characteristic amount of energy. By measuring the positions and intensities of these features, the instrument identifies the elements present and estimates their relative abundances. Major-element chemistry helps distinguish rock types and provides a chemical context for mineral observations made by other instruments [2][3]. Some instruments work on a surface contact basis, placed on a lander arm, rover or deployment mechanism. Others work at a distance, either from the surface using a laser or from orbit using natural or induced radiation [1][5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of an elemental composition analyser is to determine what the surface is made of. Its results can be used to compare the chemistry of different terrains, check whether a landing site is representative of the wider region, support the interpretation of orbital images and mineral spectra, and test models of how the Moon's crust and mantle formed. For in-situ instruments, measurements can also detect minor or volatile elements that are important for science and for later resource assessment. The Chang'e-3 APXS was used together with the VNIS spectrometer to infer both chemistry and mineralogy at one landing site [2]. Apollo 15 and 16 orbital gamma-ray and X-ray experiments mapped the major-element composition of a large part of the surface [1]. Chandrayaan-3's LIBS and APXS instruments were reported in August 2023 to have detected sulphur near the south polar landing site [5][6].
article.operating_principle:
Several measurement principles are used, and their physics differs.

Alpha backscatter was used on Surveyor 5 to 7. A radioactive alpha source irradiates the surface, and alpha particles that rebound elastically from surface nuclei lose energy in a manner that depends on the mass of the nucleus struck. Counting the energies of the returning particles therefore gives information on which elements are present [7][8][9]. This is a general physical principle; the detector and geometry of the Surveyor instrument were not confirmed from a primary document in this run.

Alpha-induced X-ray emission (APXS) combines several channels. Alpha particles excite characteristic X-rays from the sample, which a silicon-PIN detector records. Alpha particles that scatter elastically and protons from alpha-induced nuclear reactions are recorded by separate detectors, which together help identify light and heavy elements [10]. The Chang'e-3 and Chandrayaan-3 APXS units are described in the sources as alpha-source instruments, but their detailed channel configurations were not verified in this run.

Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) fires a pulsed laser at the surface. The laser vaporises a very small amount of material into a plasma, and the light emitted by the plasma is analysed by wavelength to identify elements [3][5]. ISRO described the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS as determining the chemical and mineralogical composition of the surface [3].

X-ray fluorescence and gamma-ray spectroscopy were used from orbit by the Apollo 15 and 16 Service Module experiments. Solar X-rays excite characteristic X-ray emission from the surface, and natural radioactive decay and cosmic-ray-induced nuclear reactions produce gamma rays with element-specific energies. Both were recorded by spacecraft instruments in lunar orbit [1].
article.scientific_importance: Chemical composition is central to lunar science because it constrains how the Moon formed and evolved. Surveyor 5 measured soil chemistry on the Moon in 1967 [7]. Orbital spectrometers flown on Apollo 15 and 16 produced regional maps of major elements over a large fraction of the surface [1]. Chang'e-3 APXS measurements were used to argue that the basalt at that landing site is a new type of lunar basalt, distinct from samples returned by Apollo and Luna missions [2]. A later reanalysis of the Chang'e-3 APXS data, identified in search results but not reviewed here, reported that the quantitative results are sensitive to modelling choices [see data quality notes]. Chandrayaan-3's in-situ sulphur detections are reported in press coverage and remained under detailed analysis at the time [5][6].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an elemental composition analyser. The class includes alpha-source surface instruments, laser instruments that vaporise surface material and orbital remote-sensing spectrometers. The values below are given only where a source was read in this run. Many values for the lunar examples are not publicly specified in the sources consulted, and they are not estimated here.

examples.name: Surveyor 5-7 alpha-scattering surface analyser
examples.status: Flown on the Moon on Surveyor 5 (1967); Surveyor 6 and 7 analyses reported in abstracts and secondary summaries.
examples.measurement_principle: Alpha backscatter (elastic scattering of alpha particles from a curium-242 source)
examples.description: Surveyor 5 (1967) replaced the spacecraft's surface sampler with an alpha-backscatter instrument to determine the relative abundance of chemical elements in lunar material. NASA's mission page reports that the instrument found the soil to be composed of more than half oxygen, with various amounts of silicon and aluminium. The page gives no percentages [7]. Secondary summaries describe curium-242 alpha sources and charged-particle detectors, but the number of sources, the collimation and the detector parameters were not confirmed from a primary document in this run. A Smithsonian collection record exists for the Surveyor alpha scattering auxiliary hardware [8]. An abstract record of the preliminary Surveyor VI chemical analysis was identified [9]. Secondary summaries also report that the Surveyor VII highland analysis showed much less titanium than the maria, and that the Surveyor VI result was similar to Surveyor V within experimental error. These statements were not checked against the primary papers.

examples.name: Apollo 15 and 16 Service Module gamma-ray and X-ray spectrometers
examples.status: Flown in lunar orbit on Apollo 15 and 16 (1971-1972).
examples.measurement_principle: Orbital X-ray fluorescence and gamma-ray spectroscopy
examples.description: Apollo 15 and 16 carried gamma-ray and X-ray spectrometers in their Service Modules, which remained in lunar orbit while the lander operated on the surface. The X-ray experiment targeted magnesium, aluminium and silicon and was reduced to Al/Si and Mg/Si intensity ratios. The gamma-ray experiment measured natural and cosmic-ray-induced emissions and reported abundances of thorium, uranium, potassium, iron, titanium, silicon and oxygen across major regions [1]. The 1974 conference abstract reports a large-scale compositional map of over 10 percent of the lunar surface [1]. Secondary summaries add that the Apollo 15 and 16 orbital inclinations differed, and that gamma-ray gain drifted during the missions. Those summaries were not checked against the full paper. A 2021 re-evaluation of the X-ray data was identified in search results and was not reviewed.

examples.name: Chang'e-3 Yutu rover APXS
examples.type: Lunar surface rover instrument (alpha particle X-ray spectrometer)
examples.status: Flown on the Chang'e-3 Yutu rover (2013).
examples.description: The Chang'e-3 Yutu rover carried an alpha particle X-ray spectrometer (APXS) that was used alongside the VNIS visible and near-infrared spectrometer [2]. Secondary summaries report that the APXS obtained its first X-ray fluorescence spectrum of lunar regolith in late December 2013, and that the X-ray count rate was also used to estimate the distance to the surface during deployment. Ling et al. (2015) report that the regolith at the site is extremely rich in FeO, high in CaO, intermediate in TiO2, modest in Al2O3 and poor in SiO2 [2]. The authors place the landing site on the ejecta of a fresh crater about 450 m across and argue that the local regolith represents excavated basalt of a new type [2]. The interpretation rests on a small number of measurement locations. A reanalysis found that the APXS quantification is sensitive to particle-size and modelling assumptions, and it proposed that the landing site differs from earlier detections. The full text of that reanalysis was not reviewed. The mass and power of the Chang'e-3 APXS were not verified.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover APXS and LIBS
examples.type: Lunar surface rover instruments (APXS and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy)
examples.status: Flown on the Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover (2023).
examples.measurement_principle: Alpha-induced X-ray emission (APXS) and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS)
examples.description: Chandrayaan-3's Pragyan rover carried two elemental analysis instruments, the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) and the Laser Induced Breakdown Spectroscope (LIBS) [3][4]. ISRO describes the payloads as deriving the elemental composition in the vicinity of the landing site, and lists the target elements as magnesium, aluminium, silicon, potassium, calcium, titanium and iron [3]. In late August 2023 ISRO announced that LIBS had confirmed sulphur on the lunar surface near the south pole, and that APXS had also detected sulphur and other minor elements [5][6]. Press coverage listed additional LIBS-detected elements, including chromium, manganese and oxygen. Coverage also quoted a caution that the detection came from one spot and that more data are needed [5][6]. The rover's planned operating period was about one lunar day, after which the payloads were switched off and data were relayed through the lander, according to press and secondary summaries. The instrument-level mass, dimensions and power for APXS and LIBS were not verified, and the ISRO rover figures in the landing brochure could not be retrieved in this run.

examples.name: Mars Pathfinder Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS)
examples.type: Flown Mars surface instrument (design reference; not lunar)
examples.status: Flown on Mars Pathfinder (1997); design described as a copy of an instrument flown on Vega, Phobos and Mars '96.
examples.measurement_principle: Alpha backscatter, alpha-proton reactions and alpha-induced X-ray emission (curium-244 sources)
examples.description: The Mars Pathfinder Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer is included here as a well-documented flown design of the same measurement class, operating on Mars rather than the Moon. NASA's Planetary Data System instrument description gives a mass of 570 g and dimensions of 10.5 x 8.0 x 6.5 cm [10]. The instrument used nine curium-244 alpha sources and three detector types. Silicon detectors recorded backscattered alpha particles and protons, and a Si-PIN X-ray detector with a beryllium window recorded characteristic X-rays [10]. The analysis area is a circle about 5 cm across. The description gives roughly 10 hours of integrated measurement for high-quality alpha and proton spectra, and about 3 hours for high-quality X-ray spectra [10]. The design is described as a foreign-provided copy of an instrument flown on the Russian Vega, Phobos and Mars '96 missions [10]. These numbers belong to the Mars Pathfinder unit and must not be applied to the lunar examples.

examples.name: Curiosity (Mars Science Laboratory) APXS
examples.type: Flown Mars surface instrument (image example; not lunar)
examples.status: Flown on the Curiosity rover on Mars (since 2012). Specifications not verified in this article.
examples.measurement_principle: Alpha-induced X-ray emission and related channels
examples.description:
A later Mars instrument of the same type is the APXS on NASA's Curiosity rover (Mars Science Laboratory). NASA's JPL image of the instrument, taken by the Mast Camera on sol 32 (7 September 2012 PDT), shows it with Martian terrain behind it. NASA reports that the image confirmed the APXS was not caked with dust after the rover's dusty landing [11]. The mass, dimensions and power of this instrument were not verified in this article.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The only dimensions verified in the sources consulted are those of the Mars Pathfinder APXS, 10.5 x 8.0 x 6.5 cm [10]. No verified external dimensions were found for the Surveyor, Apollo, Chang'e-3 or Chandrayaan-3 instruments. For a surface-contact instrument, the sensor head size and the distance from the head to the surface determine the analysed area. For an orbital instrument, the spacecraft bus and the detector geometry constrain the size.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only instrument mass verified in the sources consulted is 570 g for the Mars Pathfinder APXS [10]. Masses for the Surveyor alpha instrument, the Apollo 15 and 16 Service Module spectrometers, the Chang'e-3 APXS and the Chandrayaan-3 APXS and LIBS were not verified, and they are recorded as null in the JSON.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power consumption was not verified for any lunar example in the sources consulted and is not publicly specified in this article. Surface instruments share the power budget of their lander or rover, and orbital instruments share that of their spacecraft.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Elemental composition analysers face the environment of their platform. Lunar surface instruments must withstand vacuum, large temperature swings between lunar day and night, radiation and dust. Operating time is tied to the platform's power and thermal conditions. Press coverage reports that the Chandrayaan-3 payloads were switched off after the rover's planned operating period [5][6]. Surface-contact instruments need a defined standoff and a stable target area for repeatable results. Alpha-source instruments also carry radioactive-source handling and licensing requirements before launch. These requirements are standard for radioisotope sources, but the mission-specific requirements were not verified in this article. Orbital instruments must hold a stable pointing attitude and altitude during measurement [1].
article.limitations: Surface measurements describe a small area, so they may not represent a whole landing region. Alpha-based and X-ray-based surface instruments are sensitive to the surface geometry and to particle size, and their quantitative values depend on calibration and modelling. The Chang'e-3 reanalysis illustrates this sensitivity [see data quality notes]. Orbital instruments average over large footprints and cannot resolve the composition of individual rocks. A 1971 conference summary reports that Surveyor alpha-scattering analyses are usually less precise than laboratory analyses of returned samples [9]. Single-spot in-situ results, such as the Chandrayaan-3 sulphur detection, require further observations before they can be generalised [6].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: An elemental composition analyser is carried either on a lander or rover, where it needs a defined view of the surface and a stable mounting, or on an orbiter, where it looks down at the surface. The sources consulted describe the Surveyor 5, Chang'e-3 and Chandrayaan-3 instruments as lander- or rover-based, and the Apollo 15 and 16 spectrometers as Service Module instruments in lunar orbit [1][3][7].
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into the lander, rover or service module on Earth, including any handling requirements for radioactive sources where the design uses one.
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
Deliver a surface instrument to the lunar surface with a lander, or place an orbital instrument in lunar orbit within its spacecraft.
Position a surface sensor head against the target, for example by a robotic arm, a deployment mechanism or a hinge, and establish a defined distance from the surface.
Connect power, thermal control and data relay through the lander or rover, which then relays the measurements to Earth.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Surveyor 5 alpha instrument was carried on the lander in place of the surface sampler and used from the lander's surface operations [7]. The Chang'e-3 and Chandrayaan-3 instruments were carried on rovers and used after the rover had been set down. Their detailed deployment sequences were not verified here. The Apollo 15 and 16 spectrometers operated from orbit in the Service Modules [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Surveyor 5 (1967) measured soil chemistry with an alpha-backscatter instrument [7]. The Apollo 15 and 16 Service Module spectrometers mapped lunar composition from orbit [1]. Chang'e-3 (2013) and Chandrayaan-3 (2023) carried rover-based elemental analysers [2][3][5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander or rover compatibility is asserted in this article. A new elemental composition analyser would need its mass, dimensions, sensor standoff, deployment mechanism, power, thermal and data requirements compared with verified lander or rover interface specifications before any compatibility could be claimed.

article.historical_significance: Elemental composition measurements have a long history on the Moon. Surveyor 5 measured soil chemistry with an alpha-backscatter instrument in 1967 [7]. Apollo 15 and 16 orbital gamma-ray and X-ray instruments produced regional composition maps [1]. The Chang'e-3 APXS and VNIS measurements led to a proposed new basalt type at the landing site [2], a conclusion that a later reanalysis questioned. Chandrayaan-3 reported the in-situ detection of sulphur near the south pole with LIBS and APXS in 2023 [5][6]. These announcements were made during the mission, and detailed scientific analyses were still in progress when coverage was published.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name 'elemental composition analyser' covers instruments that use different physical methods, so values for Surveyor, Apollo, Chang'e-3, Chandrayaan-3 and Mars Pathfinder must not be interchanged. Mass, dimensions and power are verified in this article only for the Mars Pathfinder APXS. The Chang'e-3 composition values come from a 2015 paper whose full text could not be accessed in this run, so they are reported as summarised in the abstract record and the secondary summaries; a later reanalysis reaches different quantitative conclusions. The Chandrayaan-3 detections are reported from press announcements rather than peer-reviewed analyses. Surveyor 6 and 7 statements rely on abstract records and secondary summaries. Only one image (a Mars APXS) was verified against an official source page, and no verified lunar instrument images were found.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values have query strings and fragments removed. Only one image is included; it appears in the overview and in example 6 of the physical specifications section.

data_quality_notes: Chang'e-3 APXS composition values are taken from the abstract record and secondary summaries of Ling et al. (2015), Nature Communications 6, 8880. The Nature and Springer full-text pages redirected to a login page and could not be read in this run.

A 2021 reanalysis of the Apollo X-ray data (Gloudemans et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics 649) and a later reanalysis of the Chang'e-3 APXS data were identified in search results but not reviewed. Their conclusions are not used.

Chandrayaan-3 APXS and LIBS details come from ISRO-related news coverage and secondary summaries of August 2023. The ISRO mission page was identified in search results but its content was not retrieved. The ISRO landing brochure PDF returned HTTP 404, so its rover figures (26 kg, 50 W) were not verified and are excluded. No instrument-level mass, power or dimensions were found for APXS or LIBS.

The Surveyor 5 NASA mission page was read. The source count, collimation and detector parameters for the Surveyor alpha instrument come from secondary summaries only, because the primary NASA Surveyor report is a scanned PDF that could not be read in this run. Surveyor 6 and 7 statements are from abstract titles and summaries.

The Smithsonian collection record for the Surveyor alpha scattering auxiliary hardware was identified but returned HTTP 403 when fetched, so its content and rights were not checked. No image was taken from it.

Apollo 15 and 16 values are from the 1974 conference abstract (NTRS 19750006619). Orbital inclination, gain-drift and Al/Si ratio statements come from secondary summaries and were not verified against the full paper.

The Mars Pathfinder APXS values are from the NASA PDS instrument description, which was read directly. This is a Mars instrument and is included only as a design reference; its numbers are not applied to any lunar example.

One image is included: the NASA JPL PIA16160 portrait of the Curiosity APXS. The direct JPEG link is the one listed on the JPL source page. It was not downloaded, and the full-resolution TIFF (photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/tiff/PIA16160.tif) was not checked. The image is of a Mars instrument, not a lunar one.

No verified direct image asset was found for the lunar Surveyor, Apollo, Chang'e-3 or Chandrayaan-3 instruments, so none are included. Images were not represented by null entries, because the validator requires a direct URL for each registry image.
Lander and rover compatibility is not asserted for any example. Transportation statements are general engineering context except where a source is cited.
Research status booleans are set conservatively: specifications were not fully audited and full-resolution image downloads were not checked.
